The Cognitive Revolution

📅 02 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we externalized our muscles and built the modern world.
  • Industry observers note that we externalized our muscles and built the modern world.
  • The car is doing physical work: five thousand pounds of metal and glass moving across the San Francisco Bay Area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

Industry observers note that we externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

Most mornings I ride to work in a Waymo.

The car is doing physical work: five thousand pounds of metal and glass moving across the San Francisco Bay Area. The car is also doing cognitive work: reading the road and making predictions that result in 17x fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers.

The experience asks nothing of my muscles and nothing of my mind. Both have been externalized.

According to recent reports, this one ride encapsulates two revolutions. The physical one is 200 years old. The cognitive one has barely started.

It has been revealed that it seems the mood around that second revolution is a cocktail of optimism, skepticism and anxiety. Talk of a singularity. Recursive self-improvement. Trillion-dollar clusters. Superintelligence. Unemployment. Social disruption. A race between superpowers. Itâs dizzying.

In a recent development, my view is far from dizzying. I think we have already undergone a transition that rhymes with the AI revolution in the coming decades: the Industrial Revolution.

In a recent development, we can bifurcate work into physical work and cognitive work. Most valuable tasks necessitate both.

Industry observers note that agriculture is one of the oldest examples. Working the land took muscle, ours and our animals', for ten thousand years. It also took insight: reading the seasons, observing which seed produced which yield, etc.

It has been revealed that the two kinds of work are different. Physical work is force times distance: moving mass through space. Cognitive work is thinking. But both are scarce, have a price, and get applied to a task somebody wants done. In both cases when price collapses, supply floods in. In most cases, demand expands to meet supply.

For most of history, nearly all physical work done for humans was done by muscle, ours and animals. The chart above goes flat before the 1700s, and the flat part runs back as far as we do.

In a recent development, in the late 1700s and early 1800s things started to change. First steam, then combustion and the electric motor. Each wave took a larger share of the world's physical work. Over the course of about two centuries, physical work went from 99% biological to 99.9% machine.

Today the results are everywhere. The screen youâre reading this on. Nearly every article of clothing youâre wearing. The plane that carried you on your last trip. The lattice of ships, trains and trucks behind every ordinary product in modern life. Human muscle is a rounding error in the global energy budget.

For most of history, essentially all cognitive work was done by humans (plus a small assist from animals like the sheepdog). On top of that sat a thin mechanical sliver: tools that computed a little, like the clock or Pascal's mechanical calculator.

Then came electronic computation. Inside a century, it spread from simple calculations and spreadsheets to trillions then quadrillions of operations running 24 hours per day. Navigating your commute, processing payroll, pricing your insuranceâ¦this is all cognitive work done by machines.

The next wave is neural networks. This wave drastically expands the types of cognitive work machines can do. Just as combustion engines magnified the scope of the Industrial Revolution, neural networks are set to accelerate the Cognitive Revolution.

A century ago, 99% of cognitive work was done by humans. In the near future, 99.9% will be done by machines. Not because humans will think less, but because machines will compute much much more.

Recent findings suggest that the parallel in the two curves is stark. The Cognitive Revolution will look a lot like the Industrial Revolution. But it will be bigger and much faster. Divide the global economy by the nature of work, and cognitive and physical work could split a ~$120 trillion world economy roughly equally. The physical half has been mechanizing for 200 years. The cognitive half has barely started.

So what actually happens in a revolution like this? Letâs run it back.

The industrial age required massively scaling up input commodities: first coal and iron, then oil and steel. Iron was made by a process known as puddling. Steel was made by a process called the Bessemer process.

In a recent development, the parallel is clear: electricity and compute. The âprocessâ here are algorithms like the Transformer.

In a recent development, the providers of those components were the titans of their era. Carnegie and U.S. Steel, Rockefeller and Standard Oil. Process designers like Henry Bessemer. The modern equivalents are Jensen Huang's NVIDIA, Morris Changâs TSMC, authors of the Transformer paper, founders of the great Model Labs and the hyperscalers pouring trillions into data centers. Nations that once measured power in refining capacity will measure it in grid capacity and intelligence output.

A unit of mechanical work in 1900 cost a small fraction of what it cost in 1800. That collapse in price made mass production possible, and made the revolution universal rather than a curiosity for the rich.

The cost of cognition is collapsing faster. Intelligence per Watt has been falling more than 10x per year.

With price decline, customers will buy wildly, absurdly more intelligence.

Nobody in 1800 flew to Tokyo, shipped strawberries across a hemisphere in January, or air-conditioned Phoenix. All these are physical processes that either were impossible or impractically expensive.

According to recent reports, demand for physical work exploded once new technologies were invented and price collapsed. William Jevons identified the phenomenon in 1865: more efficient engines did not reduce Britain's coal consumption. They multiplied it.

Cognition will follow the same pattern, and here the latent demand is almost unbounded in scale. Most problems on Earth currently go un-thought-about, because thinking is expensive. A doctor has limited time and doesnât review the latest literature. A radiologist studies a scan for minutes instead of hours. A small business owner has no budget for a financial analyst.

When cognition costs approach zero, every curiosity can get a research team.

In a recent development, the amount of thinking done by machines will grow by orders of magnitude. Which raises the question, what will all that thinking be spent on?

The primal application of the Industrial Revolution was spinning textiles.

In a recent development, spinning and weaving were skilled work. Textile makers were respected in your society: years of apprenticeship, a craft guild, a trade the family had held for generations. In 1764, James Hargreaves built the Spinning Jenny, which let one person spin eight threads at once, and later eighty. Clothing prices fell rapidly and global clothing consumption exploded.

The major change was the human moving from performing the task to supervising it. One person tending a frame produced what a room of hand-spinners once had.

The primal skilled application of this era is AI coding. Writing software is our era's elite craft: highly skilled, highly paid, a decade to master. And it is the first cognitive task where the pattern has fully flipped. The machine now completes most of the work, and the engineer's job is to direct, review and correct it. Itâs no accident that this is where the Cognitive Revolution found its first commercial traction.

Industry observers note that while textiles kicked off the industrial revolution, they did not define it. The ultimate innovation of the industrial revolution was the automobile: a civilization grew around it, including suburbs, highways, supply chains, and the entire geography of modern life.

Sources indicate that coding agents are our Spinning Jennies: the first act, automating a skilled cognitive task. The automobile of this revolution has probably not been built yet. It will be something that was impossible while thinking was scarce.

It has been revealed that my candidates: science conducted at machine speed, the personal agent that serves your life the way a chief of staff organizes a CEO's, or something in how humans connect and coordinate. In 1800, the automobile would have been hard to predict.

In a recent development, in 1800, over 75% of American workers worked the land. Machines came for that work. Today, farming is about 1% of U.S. employment. By the pessimists' arithmetic, over 74% of the country should be unemployed.

Sources indicate that instead we invented work no farmer in 1800 could have named. Radiologist. Software engineer. Podcast producer. Flight attendant. The machines did not end labor. They eliminated categories of work and expanded the total amount of it. There are more people employed today than at any point in human history, and they are vastly richer than their ancestors. All of my ancestors worked in agriculture 100 years ago. I knew all four of my grandparents, all of whom were born to farming families. None of them finished their lives in agriculture. All of them considered the non-agricultural work they did at the end of their lives more pleasant and prosperous than the hard agricultural work their families had done for generations.

Industry observers note that the same is taking shape in the Cognitive revolution. Despite the âspinning Jennyâ phenomena in AI coding, data supports that demand for software engineers, the most AI exposed occupation was accelerating higher, has inflected. In the coming week, we proposal to share data supporting inflections in hiring in other areas being transformed by AI, including Legal Services and Financial Services.

According to recent reports, machines doing cognitive work will not mean humans stop doing cognitive work any more than the tractor meant humans stopped doing physical things. The specific tasks change. The junior analyst who builds the model by hand becomes the person directing a hundred models. Further, categories of work we cannot right now name will grow the way "engineer" became a job following the invention of the engine during the Industrial Revolution.

Like in the industrial revolution, the aggregate story will be triumphant. But, the individual story will frequently not be. The handloom weavers of Lancashire were not retrained into locomotive engineers. Many of them simply lost, and their losses spanned a generation. The economic historian Robert Allen gave the period a name: Engels' pause. Between 1780 and 1840, British output per worker rose 46%. Real wages rose 12%.

According to recent reports, luddites were not wrong about their own lives, but about their childrenâs and grandchildren's. Between 1840 and 1900, British output per worker rose 90% and real wages rose 123%. Wages caught up to productivity, and then outran it.

A pause is not a foregone conclusion. Mark Zuckerberg put this well recently: âThere is no rule that AI must increase automation faster than it increases individuals' capabilities or demand for upcoming skills.â Humanityâs demand for new skills, for better and worse, will be insatiable.The difference this time is speed. The Industrial Revolution gave a farmhand's son forty years to become a factory hand. This revolution may offer five. Society's shock absorbers, like education, retraining, and safety nets, were designed for the old clock. The central policy question of the next two decades is whether we can help humans transform as fast as the jobs do.

The Industrial Revolution created the modern education system, in at least two ways.

First, it made mass education possible. When most of humanity had to work the fields, children were labor. Machines taking over the physical work is what freed children to sit in classrooms and freed societies to fund them. The modern university exists because society no longer needed every able body in the field, and could redirect a civilization's youth toward cognitive skill-building instead.

Sources indicate that second, and less flatteringly, it shaped what education became. The factory needed workers who could read instructions, do arithmetic, show up on time and perform standardized tasks in synchronized shifts. So we built schools that look suspiciously like factories: Bells. Rows. Fixed schedules. Batch processing by age. Standardized outputs. Mass education was, in large part, industrial job training.

Recent findings suggest that the Cognitive Revolution upends both of these dynamics. If machines do the cognition, the factory-model school is the equivalent of training for hand-spinning. But the deeper change is on the delivery side. For all of history, the binding constraint on education was the ratio of teachers to students. Benjamin Bloom quantified the cost of that constraint in 1984: the average student tutored one-to-one with mastery learning outperformed 98% of students in a conventional classroom.

That constraint is dissolving. The marginal cost of an infinitely patient, endlessly knowledgeable tutor is approaching zero. Hybrid human-AI tutors are found to be more effective and less costly than traditional education. Further, fresh hybrid AI approaches could help spread education in parts of the world where public education has been prohibitively expensive.

Modern medicine was also built by the industrial revolution. Mass production gave us penicillin at scale, refrigeration that made vaccines deliverable, and the chemical industry that spawned the pharmaceutical industry.

The Cognitive Revolution pushes this much further. Drug discovery is a search across a space too large for humans to comprehend, which is exactly the work that scales best when cognition gets cheap. By predicting structures for virtually every known protein, AlphaFold solved a challenge where even minor breakthroughs previously demanded entire lifelong careers.Thousands of diseases currently have no treatment, not because they are unsolvable but because the cost of investigating each was never justified by the number of patients. When that cost collapses, the long tail becomes addressable the way every other latent demand does.

Curing disease has been the ambition of every generation of physicians. This is the first generation where the binding constraint is no longer how many of them there are.

According to recent reports, then there are the doctors in clinical practice. We face a massive shortage of physicians both in the United States and globally, with demand far exceeding supply. This issue is deeply personal to me, as I have long seen healthcare workers in my family stretched thin attempting to meet patient needs. Cheaper, accessible cognitive tools will not lead to doctors taking time off; instead, they will allow more patients to receive higher-quality care. Given the virtually limitless demand for better healthcare, scalable intelligence can help shift our medical model from reactive treatment to proactive care.The Shape of Daily Life.

Sources indicate that beyond work and school, the Industrial Revolution changed the texture of ordinary life so thoroughly that we now mistake its artifacts for human nature. The Cognitive Revolution will change them once again.

Sources indicate that clock time. Before factories, rural work followed seasons and sunlight. But a factory owner needed hundreds of people to start and stop simultaneously. The machine ran on a schedule, so the humans had to. Rigid shifts, the workday, the work week, modern timekeeping itself: these are industrial inventions, barely two centuries old. The Cognitive Revolution loosens their grip. When your machine colleagues work continuously and asynchronously, there is no reason for a hundred humans to think in unison from nine to five. Work drifts back toward task rhythms rather than clock rhythms.

Home and Work. Work happened in and around the home for most of human history: the farm, the cottage workshop, the family trade. Industrialization pulled the workplace out of domestic space because the work had to happen where the machine was. The daily commute is the residue of that separation. The Cognitive Revolution reverses it, because the machine now lives everywhere and one of the most powerful tools in history fits in your pocket. Home and work are recombining.

It has been revealed that global trade and power. Industrial nations imported raw materials and exported finished goods, an asymmetry that drove imperialism. The new raw materials are energy, compute and algorithms. The finished good is intelligence. The last time this asymmetry appeared, it defined a century of international order and disorder: the same industrial base that laid rail and poured steel also eventually created atomic bombs. Intelligence will be dual-use in the same way, and faster. The Industrial Revolution lifted humanity, but its safeguards arrived late. This time we should try to be earlier.

Follow the thread and you eventually arrive at the real question underneath the anxiety about AI: If the machines do the thinking, what are we for?

The last revolution already answered the physical version. At the end of the Industrial Revolution, humans did not stop moving their bodies. We remained embodied creatures.

Proportionally, fewer of us work intense physical jobs. However, far more of us move for sport and purpose: we run marathons, climb mountains, and pay for the privilege of holding yoga poses in uncomfortably hot rooms. Along the way, we created sports-leagues and even the modern Olympics were the result of the Industrial Revolution.

Sources indicate that cognition will make the same migration. Chess is a clean example. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 and Kasparov later half-jokingly described himself as the first knowledge worker whose job was threatened by a machine. Chess did not die. More people play it today than at any point in history. When AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, researchers found that the novelty of moves played by human Go professionals increased significantly afterward. Superhuman machines made human play more creative, not less. The âcentaurâ era of machine-human collaboration was brief, but the human era never ended.

Critics of this essay will argue that âthis time is different.â Specifically, they will point out that humans were the smartest animals on earth and that this is the first time something uniquely human is displaced by a machine. That is incorrect. It is incorrect for at least two reasons. First, thinking is not uniquely human. Animals think. Even nature follows complex and âintelligentâ patterns. Second, there are many uniquely human skills that machines exceed already. For example, making fire is strictly a human skillâ¦and now your stove does it with the press of a button. Same with writing and transferring information (the internet). Same with making tools (us and chimpanzees), but now machines make most of our tools. And then Einstein reinvented it completely-- humans making a comeback -- with a latest human thought experiment that was needed to accurately plot the orbit of Mercury! Flight was a super-human task until airplanes made it accessible. This time is different, but not that different.What stays economically human the longest is what was never really cognition to begin with: wanting things, choosing between them, being accountable for the choice, and being trusted by other people. The machine can draft the treaty. Someone still has to sign it. Over 2500 years ago, Greek philosopher Protagaros wrote "Man is the measure of all things." Indeed, value as we experience it is in what we offer to other people.

In a recent development, stand far enough back and this is all one story. For all of history, humans did the work: with our muscles and with our minds. Twice, we built machines that took the work and externalized it to machines.

The first time, we were terrified, and the fear was short-term justified and long-term wrong. The world after the machines took most of the physical work was profoundly more abundant, healthy  and humane.

The same trade is on the table now, at greater scale and higher speed. The Cognitive Revolution will be turbulent, unevenly distributed, and deeply uncomfortable . And, it will end the way the last one did: with the world unrecognizably better, its results so completely woven into daily life that our grandchildren will live inside them.

We have made this trip before.This time, we can navigate it with our eyes open: shaping the transition calmly, sharing the prosperity, and remembering that the goal of externalizing our minds is ultimately to elevate our humanity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

Controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

In a recent development, every large enterprise now has an AI mandate. Very few know exactly what happens when an agent is granted access to enterprise systems and data. What exactly will it be able to reach? How will we know what it did with it? These questions â not model quality, not cost, not talent â are the reason so many enterprise AI programs stay stuck in pilots. Cymphony was built to answer them.

It has been revealed that employees increasingly work together with AI agents to execute day-to-day work. But the typical agent is nothing like an employee. It can be provisioned in minutes rather than hired over weeks. It works continuously. And it can reach across far more systems, data, and capability than an individual person. Every one of those properties is what makes an AI agent worth deploying â and every one of them is what makes a security team say no.

Governance and security are already major barriers to AI adoption, with 40% of enterprises expected to demote or decommission autonomous AI agents over governance concerns by next year. That is not a prediction about AI failing to work. Itâs about enterprises pulling back working agents because they cannot see or control what those agents reaching. The fundamental challenge is not utility, but accountability.

Recent findings suggest that for decades, security teams have built tools around two separate concerns: where sensitive data lives, and who has access. The first produced the tools that watch files, inboxes, and databases for leaks. The second produced the identity industry. But both assume the "who"s are human employees.

Sources indicate that AI broke that assumption. An identity tool can tell you an agent exists. A data tool can tell you a file is sensitive. Neither can tell you that a given agent, acting on behalf of a given employee, can reach that file right now. Identity security and data security are no longer separable.

In a recent development, cymphony continuously maps both employees and agents across an enterprise, graphing who and what can reach which systems and information. It is a difficult engineering problem: the same person routinely holds a dozen different accounts scattered across systems that were never designed to talk to each other, and agents inherit access from the humans and applications that spawned them. Stitching all of that back into one accurate picture requires more than a dashboard that aggregates alerts.

What we love about working with co-founders Shy Dekel, Idan Berkovits, and Edi Gotlieb is their instinct to build not for the alert but for the workflow. Instead of stopping at detection and leaving a security analyst to figure out what to do next, Cymphony pushes further â recommending and even automating remediation, and coordinating with the people who need to take action.

Sources indicate that enterprise customers including Syngenta, KKR, Cass Information Systems, and Athennian are already seeing results. Sequoia is also a happy customer. We are proud to have led Cymphonyâs seed round, and to now co-lead their Series A.

We met Shy, Idan, and Edi through Sequoia's Israel network, introduced separately by two people in our orbit who each said some version of the same thing: these three had spent their careers on hard, unglamorous security problem many founders avoid, and they were building something different around it. All three came out of Israel's elite Talpiot program. All three have deep experience in this space: Shy led the cyber department for Unit 8200, Idan ran a research group in the Office of the Prime Minister and won an Israel Defense Prize, and Edi built hardware at Apple and at the Israeli Ministry of Defense. Every large enterprise software firm has been built on a transition: the underlying unit of work changes, and the old categories are no longer the right shape. Cloud changed where software ran, and security rebuilt itself around it. Mobile changed what an endpoint was, and it rebuilt itself again. Each time, the companies that offered visibility and control over what came next eventually became infrastructure everyone else took for granted.

AI is no exception, albeit the first shift where the new unit of work can act on its own. The tech giant that lets an enterprise say yes to agents â confidently, at scale, with a record of what they did â will be not just a feature inside the AI stack, but a precondition for it. We think Cymphony is building that layer, and we are glad to be part of it.

By Bogomil Balkansky, Dean Meyer and David Cahn.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

Recent findings suggest that AI took the digital world by storm in a few short years, and we are still only scratching the surface. Each time digital AI has moved to a new phase, from pretraining to reinforcement learning to deployment, spend on compute and data has not plateaued. It has accelerated.

Industry observers note that bringing AI into the physical world will be a wave of comparable importance to digital AI, if not larger, but the infrastructure required to get there will be harder to build and scale, and that already shows at every stage. In pretraining, language models benefited from decades of text accumulated on the internet. Robotics has no comparable, ready-made collection of the movements, interactions and sensory information needed to understand the physical world. That experience has to be captured before it can be learned from. In reinforcement learning and deployment, digital AI operates in clean, structured environments that are easy to scale. Physical AI lives in the noisy, unpredictable, operationally complex reality of the real world. It operates in the field, not in the cloud.

In a recent development, to reach physical AGI, the industry has to build both the brain and the body. The brain needs data that wasnât collected. The body needs someone doing the work on the ground.

That is the mission Josh, Jason and the Mecka AI team have taken on: helping physical AI labs, robotics companies and end enterprises reach physical AGI and put it to use, by being their partner for training data, reinforcement learning, and deployment.

Delivering on this mission requires developing several muscles across disciplines, all at once and all at scale:.

Research: Identify the next wave in robotics, and what it will require, before it arrives.

Hardware: Once you see the wave, design the bespoke hardware and wearables to capture the data, then manufacture them fast, economically, and at scale.

Operations: Run large-scale global operations to collect the data. Volume alone is not enough; the data has to span every job in every industry.

Software and digital AI: Turn the raw output, which is far more voluminous and complex than text (e.g., multi-camera video, body and hand tracking, sensor streams), into high-quality, training-ready data.

Deployment: Put robots in front of end customers, for reinforcement learning and production deployment.

Each of these muscles is difficult to develop on its own, but to win, you need not one but all of them, working together and at scale. Training data today, for example, has to be high volume AND high diversity AND high quality AND delivered fast AND at a good price. It is easy to do one of these at small volume, but it is incredibly difficult to do all of them at once and at scale, and that is what it takes to help partners reach physical AGI. In the same way, it is easy to start a food delivery business that delivers a single dish from one restaurant to one apartment block, but it is incredibly difficult to scale it into a DoorDash.

Recent findings suggest that mecka's founders and team understood this and moved fast to build all five muscles, finding differentiated edge in each and executing on it. The result is a strong, scalable and flexible platform that has enabled them to win over many of the leading AI labs and robotics companies and swiftly become the emerging leader of this category.

Recent findings suggest that what drew us to Mecka is not that they made the right bet on the right form of data (although they did). Robotics is still early relative to digital AI. The form factor of the data might change. The form factor of the robots might change. What matters is that they built the machine that scales with the industry and its partners; regardless of how the input changes over time, the output will be what their partners want. In the same way, DoorDash built a system where, whether the input is a pizza or a laptop, the customer gets the same delightful delivery experience. And when something in the physical world has high barriers to scale, it is an opportunity for the right team to build a large, durable business with moats.

That is why we are excited to back Josh, Jason and their fast-growing team. We see in them the special ingredients that will keep compounding over the long term to win this category and help their partners advance the mission of building and deploying robots at scale around the world.

And it is why others have joined us, from strategics like NVIDIA, Samsung, Microsoft and Qualcomm to the founders and operators who scaled some of the most defining companies of their generation and excel in many of the disciplines required in Meckaâs business: Tony Xu, founder and CEO of DoorDash; Frank Slootman, former CEO of ServiceNow and Snowflake; Milan Kovac, former head of Optimus at Tesla; Christopher Payne, former President & COO of Doordash; Jonathan Chadwick, former COO and CFO of VMware and board member at Databricks; and many more.Photo by S72 Business Portraits.

By Anas Biad, Pat Grady and Brian Halligan.

  • A Figma engineer is suing the design software company and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.
  • District Court for the Southern District of Latest York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints.
  • “Figma was my dream tech giant for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Figma engineer is suing the design software company and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Latest York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints. Park, who joined Figma in 2022, alleges the company’s response damaged her career, compensation, and mental health. The lawsuit also alleges that Park, who is Asian, faced racial and gender discrimination, including performance criticism based on stereotypes that Asian women are meek, timid, and conflict-averse.

“Figma was my dream tech giant for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed. “It was a place where I felt that I could level up in my career, working on a lot of really cool, interesting things at scale.”.

Industry observers note that park is seeking damages, a jury trial, and a court order prohibiting Figma from requiring employees who report harassment to confront their alleged harassers. She also wants the tech giant to adopt and enforce a process for investigating harassment complaints promptly and confidentially.

When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Figma said, “Figma does not tolerate discrimination or harassment. Figma also does not tolerate extortion. These claims have no merit, and we will present the facts in court.”.

Park told TechCrunch she initially had faith in Figma’s complaint process, expecting that if she documented the alleged harassment and reported it to the right people, the company would act. But as an engineer in a male-dominated field, Park told TechCrunch, “I don’t feel that they took me seriously throughout this process.”.

Park, who is still employed at Figma, joined its San Francisco office in October 2022. Within weeks, her onboarding mentor — a fellow engineer — asked her on a date and continued pursuing her after she declined, Park alleges. She initially feared reporting him, worrying that her manager would “dismiss her reports or view her as the problem,” according to the lawsuit.

Recent findings suggest that park claims she tried to avoid her onboarding mentor. In early 2023, for example, she delayed choosing a work project until he had picked one. When her manager criticized her for not being a “team player,” Park explained that she was trying to avoid the colleague she accused of harassment, according to the suit.

Her manager allegedly dismissed her concerns, saying he had “met his wife at work too” and treating the behavior as “harmless flirtation.” When Park asked to be kept off projects with the onboarding mentor, HR allegedly instructed her to confront him directly about his behavior.

Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit ties that response to Figma’s culture of direct feedback, which Park alleges Field established and enforced. It indicates the organization’s People organization trains managers to direct employees, including those reporting harassment, to give feedback directly to the person involved.

Sources indicate that in March 2023, her manager assigned him to a major project she was leading, despite her request to be separated from him. Park told her manager that she would “figure it out,” but alleges that having to work with him affected her performance. Her manager gave her a 2 out of 5 on her performance review, criticizing her for not speaking up enough or engaging with others and for lacking presence. Park was put on a coaching plan, which she completed in late 2023.

Changing managers didn’t help, according to the lawsuit. Her second manager also refused to separate them, allegedly telling Park that someone at her level should be able to resolve conflicts with teammates and that separating them would be “avoiding the problem.” Like her previous manager, he allegedly pointed out that he had met his partner at work.

Park alleges the harassment continued throughout 2023.

In April 2024, she transferred to another team, a move she claims set back her career by resetting her performance and promotion timeline.

On her new team, which had more women, Park mentioned she felt better and no longer had to work with her alleged harasser. Her performance reviews improved, but in late 2025, she alleges another incident of sexual harassment, this time by her new manager.

The incident followed a night out for drinks with her wife and two teammates, including her manager. The next day, during a team lunch, the manager allegedly noted Park’s sex life had been discussed the previous evening. Park, who said no such conversation had occurred in her or her wife’s presence, felt “horrified and humiliated” by comments she believed fetishized queer relationships.

A colleague reported the comments to HR as sexual harassment, according to the suit. Weeks later, Park’s manager apologized in a Slack message, saying she didn’t recall what she had noted. When Park sought HR’s guidance, she was again told to address the matter directly with her manager.

During their conversation, the manager allegedly became defensive, and the encounter left Park feeling “crushed, anxious, and vulnerable.” The manager also allegedly remarked she would never make such a comment because she had “a lot of gay friends.”.

The manager told HR that they had agreed it was a misunderstanding. HR closed its investigation without interviewing witnesses, according to the suit, even though Park disputed her manager’s account.

“Requiring an employee to confront her harasser as the price of complaining — and then closing her complaint — would dissuade a reasonable employee from complaining at all,” the suit mentioned.

Park alleges her manager retaliated by publicly berating her, sometimes so aggressively that colleagues intervened or checked on her afterward, according to the lawsuit. The suit also alleges that other teammates left the team over concerns about the manager’s behavior.

Park again complained to HR about “escalating retaliation” and expressed concern the manager would “derail her career.” HR allegedly defended the manager’s conduct, saying the manager was “within her reasonable authority” and again instructed Park to address her concerns directly with the manager.

In early 2026, Park received another low performance review and a reduced bonus. The lawsuit alleges that similarly situated men continued to receive promotions, raises, and bonuses. When Park reported the negative performance review to HR in March, she was allegedly told her sexual harassment complaint against her manager could not be “substantiated.”.

Park took medical leave in March to receive treatment for PTSD symptoms and generalized anxiety. Cleared to return to work in June, she was prescribed workplace accommodations, including a graduated work schedule and mandatory remote workdays.

Park told TechCrunch that Figma approved the accommodations but had not implemented them at the time she returned to work. In July, Park and her lawyers notified Figma of their intent to pursue legal action.

According to recent reports, “It’s really scary for me,” she noted about taking legal action. “I don’t know what’s going to happen next with this, I don’t know what the outcome is going to be, but at least it feels like this is my chance to do the right thing.”.

This piece was updated to clarify when Park remarked Figma implemented the recommendations from her medical professionals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.

The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.

Industry observers note that amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the organization is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.

By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the organization tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.

It has been revealed that in its announcement, Amazon remarked it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the organization offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.

Sources indicate that one way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.

In a recent development, annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.

In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”.

Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, mentioned on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically key acquisitions in many, many years.”.

Within 24 hours of launch on September 15, TypeSafeâs first model, Jev, became the fastest-adopted model in Vercelâs AI Gateway history.   • Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta revealed a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, pinterest declared this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one latest feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.

The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.

Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta revealed a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.

WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.

But when it comes to AI-generated content filling owners’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.

This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to people under 18.

Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into people’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the firm introduced in 2025, are enabled.

Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.

The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era.
  • According to recent reports, “Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch.
  • Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.

According to recent reports, “Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”.

It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.

That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.

Recent findings suggest that “Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he mentioned. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”.

According to recent reports, both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.

According to recent reports, G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that firm, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.

According to recent reports, the venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.

According to recent reports, “The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter stated. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”.

In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a newly introduced generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio manufacturer Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.

Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter noted they should start thinking about them now.

“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber and Nuro have started testing driverless Lucid Gravity SUVs on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area more than six months after receiving the permit that allowed the companies to pull the human safety driver from behind the wheel.

The companies will soon begin offering driverless rides to employees in the final lead-up to launching a commercial robotaxi service in the first quarter of 2027.

The milestone comes just 16 months after Uber confirmed an ambitious blueprint to launch a premium robotaxi service using Lucid electric vehicles outfitted with autonomous vehicle technology developed by startup Nuro.

Sources indicate that that plan came with hefty investments in both companies and much-needed endorsements of their respective products. Uber initially agreed to invest $300 million in Lucid — a figure that has since ballooned to $500 million. Uber also agreed to invest nearly $500 million in Nuro, TechCrunch previously reported, citing sources familiar with the deal.

The agreement provided both Lucid and Nuro with boosts beyond the obvious capital injection. Uber agreed to buy at least 20,000 of Lucid Gravity SUVs over the next six years (a figure that later popped to at least 35,000 vehicles), giving the struggling EV maker a more predictable source of revenue. Nuro, meanwhile, was less than a year removed from announcing a risky, but necessary pivot away from developing driverless delivery vehicles and toward licensing its autonomous vehicle technology to automakers and mobility companies.

It has been revealed that nuro has spent nearly a year testing the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with a human safety operator behind the wheel. The California Department of Motor Vehicles, the agency that regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, granted Nuro a driverless AV permit in May 2026.

Recent findings suggest that uber and Nuro are also testing autonomous vehicles on public roads in Houston with human safety operators behind the wheel. Nuro is supplementing that on-road testing with closed-course testing and simulation to validate the self-driving system before opening the robotaxis to the public. The companies’ combined engineering fleet of autonomous vehicles, which stood at 100 AVs earlier this year, is expanding as Lucid begins manufacturing the first production versions of the robotaxis at its Arizona factory.

Industry observers note that the Lucid Gravity robotaxi, unveiled in January 2026, is outfitted with high-resolution cameras, solid-state lidar sensors, and radars that help the self-driving system perceive the real-world environment and operate in it. Uber, which will own and operate the fleet, has focused its efforts on the in-cabin experience, including how riders will interact with the vehicle.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform.
  • Tidal stated it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year.
  • Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The manufacturer said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision.

Tidal stated it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the newly introduced rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day.

Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.

The company mentioned it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.

Industry observers note that the move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, noted that it will introduce a toggle to let people filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this concern, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures.

Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, said on X.

In a recent development, A few months ago, @Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists. But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done….

The tech giant said that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and fresh monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, instagram people can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company confirmed on Tuesday. The social media network indicates users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.

In a recent development, the fresh integration gets rid of the need for customers to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.

Consumers can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.

Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.

Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android customers in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.

It has been revealed that meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.

Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.

Meta indicates that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram. Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

Partnering with Blacksmith

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.
  • JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.
  • Industry observers note that software development has a new bottleneck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

Industry observers note that software development has a new bottleneck. Writing code is no longer the hard part; trusting it is. Coding agents now produce more code than any team can read or any existing system can verify. Led by co-founders Aditya Jayaprakash (JP), Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, Blacksmith is building infrastructure that can.

Last month, Anthropicâs engineering team described what happened as their own usage of coding agents scaled. Engineers began shipping roughly eight times as much code per quarter. Their test suite grew tenfold. The volume of continuous integration (CI) jobs, the builds and tests that check every change before it reaches production, grew 25x in six months. Anthropic is very far along the curve, but is on the same curve as every firm, and its advice to the rest of the industry was to blueprint for 25x the CI load within two quarters.

For decades, software development scaled as a function of engineering capacity. Developers were the scarce resource. Shipping more meant hiring more. That has changed. Developers now direct fleets of coding agents that work in parallel, around the clock and increasingly autonomously. These agents do not produce finished work. They produce attemptsâa patch, a test, a migration, a throwaway branchâeach iterating against a test suite until it is ready to merge. Meanwhile, the quiet backbone of software development that validates and tests code has not changed.

Validating code has also never been more important. AI coding tasks produce large volumes of security flaws, and the same model capabilities that write the code now make those flaws more dangerous. The system that was supposed to catch them is straining right as developers need it the most. With the scale and velocity of this shift, the constraint in software has moved from writing code to proving it works and is safe.

This is the problem Blacksmith set out to solve. The team started with speeding up CI. With a one-line change in a workflow file, developers using Blacksmith see their CI jobs complete twice as fast and at 60% lower cost on average. Underneath a simple product experience is a stack purpose-built from the bare metal up, designed to absorb demand spikes from customers and get faster and more efficient as it scales.

Developers have noticed. The business has seen explosive growth this year. More than 10,000 companies are using Blacksmith, up from 700 a year ago. Weekly CI jobs are up 18x, from 5 million to 90 million, in 2026 alone. And ARR has grown 17x over the same time period, with the largest customers now spending more than $1M per year.

Much of our conviction in Blacksmith is driven by the team behind it. Co-founders JP, Aayush and Maru have known each other since their undergraduate years at the University of Waterloo, and developed a maniacal focus on hyper-performant systems at Cockroach Labs and Faire. They founded Blacksmith in 2024, as autocomplete was giving way to coding assistants, on the conviction that the volume of code needing to be tested would go up by orders of magnitude. For the rest of the world, the future became clear in 2026 with the arrival of truly autonomous coding agents, but Blacksmith had already been building for it. The Blacksmith team is talent-dense and is growing swiftly. The roadmap is exciting, with several releases planned in the coming months.

It has been revealed that we are proud to lead Blacksmithâs Series C. The world is about to run far more code than it has ever written, and someone has to make sure it works. We look forward to supporting JP, Aayush and Maru as they build infrastructure that runs at agent speed, in validation and beyond.

By Shaun Maguire, Sonya Huang, James Flynn and Carl Eschenbach.

Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet.
  • While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect.
  • According to recent reports, the iPad app isn’t the tech giant’s only enhancement in the latest release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight revision, the company rolled out a substantial-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.

While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.

According to recent reports, the iPad app isn’t the tech giant’s only enhancement in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.

Sources indicate that in addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson notes the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.

Sources indicate that the update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.

Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg claims the tech giant believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the U.K.
  • National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) noted it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses.
  • The NCSC notes that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are upcoming, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.

The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) noted it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post.

The NCSC notes that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are upcoming, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.

It has been revealed that the rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.

While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.

“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.

The unit mentioned that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.

The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”.

The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, U.S. officials suspect Iranian hackers may be behind as many as 50 cyberattacks targeting shipping vessels in recent weeks, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.

The ships carrying oil, liquefied gas, and other explosive chemicals were hacked as they traveled across Asia and Europe. Several oil tankers headed toward the U.S. coast in August also had their navigation systems breached, prompting cybersecurity teams within the FBI and Coast Guard to board the vessels.

The report said officials are investigating if Iran is expanding its recent wave of hacks against the U.S. by targeting large vessels to sow fear among shippers, disrupt routes, or to cause an explosion at a port. (Ships have backup controls in the event that automated systems are hacked or fail.).

According to recent reports, hackers may have been abusing a bug dubbed FortiBleed, which allows hackers to break into networks by compromising vulnerable Fortinet-made routers. A joint FBI-Coast Guard security alert from September warned that Fortinet routers are used on shipping vessels.

Sources indicate that iran has been firing back on all sides since the start of the U.S./Israel-led war earlier this year, which killed the country’s supreme leader. Many of Iran’s retaliations have been in the form of cyberattacks, with U.S. officials blaming Iran for hacks targeting hundreds of American water providers and U.S. medical tech companies.

A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the shipping hacks or whether it had a more accurate figure.

Partnering with Edelbyte: Data Infrastructure That Keeps Up With AI's Curiosity

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI agents will ask far more questions of a firm's data than people ever did.
  • AI agents will ask far more questions of a organization's data than people ever did.
  • According to recent reports, last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI agents will ask far more questions of a firm's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

AI agents will ask far more questions of a organization's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

According to recent reports, last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft. This was the only introduction to a founding team weâd ever received from Roy, and we paid attention.

The people Roy wanted us to meet had built Kusto, a data engine that started more than a decade ago as a small incubation project inside Microsoft. Named after the oceanographer Jacques Cousteau because it was built for diving into oceans of data, Kusto was designed to get answers from enormous volumes of fast-arriving data, such as logs, telemetry and security events, in seconds rather than hours. It ran on a query language simple enough that anyone, not just substantial-data engineers, could use it. And it worked so well that it became the data engine underneath Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender and Azure Monitor, and was eventually offered to customers as Azure Data Explorer. Security teams in particular loved it, which is how Roy became one of its biggest champions. When we spoke with customers, large enterprises and fast-growing startups alike told us two things: it was game-changing data technology, and the team behind it was among the best theyâd ever worked with.

Avner Aharoni, Evgeney Ryzhyk, Alexander Sloutsky and Yoni Leibowitz were that team. Evgeney invented the Kusto engine and its query language, then rebuilt it three times, making it faster and cheaper with each iteration. Alexander turned half-formed ideas into finished features seemingly overnight, and Yoni made sure every complex design was fully thought through, starting before a line of code was ever written. Avner, who spent a quarter century at Microsoft, hustled Kusto from project to a globally beloved product. Their new company, Edelbyte, builds on this success. We are proud to have led their seed round and to be their partners.

Recent findings suggest that in B2B technology, this is a proven playbook: a team develops a solution inside a large company and then splits off to build it independently. Itâs the origin story of Sequoia portfolio companies such as Confluent, whose founders created Kafka at LinkedIn, and Temporal, whose founders built Cadence at Uber. Edelbyte now follows the same path.

But Edelbyte is not simply Kusto rebuilt for a fourth time; it is a rethinking, from first principles, of what a data platform should look like in the age of AI. With every major shift in computing, the way software is built changes, and the data infrastructure underneath it has to change too. Data platforms were designed around human owners, and there is a natural limit on the number of questions one person can type in a day. That made the trade-offs, such as keeping less history so queries stay fast, asking fewer questions so the bill stays reasonable, and building the product inside whichever cloud the database happens to run in, easier to tolerate.

In a recent development, but an AI agent investigating a problem is like a whole team of curious analysts who never get tired, testing multiple hypotheses concurrently. One agent might fire off fifty queries where a person would run one. And at that scale, rationing and trade-offs rapidly constrain the true promise of AI. An agent is only as useful as the questions it can afford to ask, and what it can afford is decided in the data layer.

Edelbyte keeps detailed history queryable at interactive speed, scales as data volumes and query demand grow, and gives people, applications and AI agents governed access to the same data. It brings search and analytics, which have historically been stitched together from separate systems at significant cost and complexity, together in a single platform. And it runs wherever you need it: in the cloud or on premises, managed or self-hosted.

Recent findings suggest that the result is exactly what an AI-heavy workload needs: no more rationing curiosity, whether it comes from a person or an agent. Already, customers are seeing dramatic increases in efficiency, including tenfold increases in queries with no increase in budget.

Industry observers note that data platforms are among the most durable and lucrative businesses in technology, because data has gravity; once it accumulates in one place it rarely moves. Each era produces its own winners, and we believe the AI era will be won by the platform that lets builders, and the agents working for them, ask as many questions as they want without worrying about the speed or the bill. Edelbyte is building just such a platform, and we are thrilled to be part of the journey.

By Bogomil Balkansky, Dean Meyer and David Cahn.

💡 Key Takeaways
